input.question: An English speaker in 2016 can understand a 200 year old book from 1816 with relative ease. Would An English speaker from 1816 be able to understand Shakespeare's then 200 year old plays just as easily?
input.ground_truth: It's unlikely, but only because Shakespeare's locution wasn't customary in his time, but peculiar even then (source: any introduction to a recent edition of a Shakespeare work). If you were to switch this question to some other author of the same period, though, I'm not sure. Edit: I also want to challenge the claim that we can understand texts from 1816 with relative ease. Academics can, but can most English speakers really deal with the crazy punctuation, tortuously long sentences, and GRE-level vocabulary?

Okay! Imagine you have a toy from 20 years ago. You can still play with it and understand how it works because toys don’t change that much.

But let’s talk about words and stories. In 2016, if you read a book from 1816, the words might look a little old, but you can still understand most of them because English doesn’t change super fast.

Now, let’s go back to 1816. People then spoke and wrote differently. If someone from 1816 tried to read a play by Shakespeare, who wrote around 200 years before (in the 1600s), the words and the way people talked would sound really, really strange to them. It would be like trying to understand a robot’s language! They might not understand a lot of the words or how people talked back then.

So, it’s harder for the old person to understand the very old story, but it’s easier for us to understand things that are only 200 years old.
